title: The Tower of Babel and the Line to Abram
summary: The whole world speaks one language, and people settle in the plain of Shinar, where they decide to build a city and a tower reaching to the heavens to make a name for themselves and avoid being scattered. The LORD comes down, confuses their language, and scatters them over the earth, and the city is called Babel. The chapter then traces the line of Shem for ten generations to Terah, whose son Abram marries Sarai, who is barren, and whose family sets out from Ur for Canaan but settles in Haran.
story: This chapter closes the Bible's account of the world's beginnings and opens the door to Abraham. The first nine verses are the last of the great stories of human rebellion in Genesis 1 to 11, after the fall, Cain's murder, and the corruption before the flood. This time the sin is collective: humanity unites to build its own greatness and security apart from God. God's judgment scatters them, as chapter 10 has already described. Then the genealogy narrows from all nations to one line, from Shem to Terah, and ends with a family on the move and a woman who cannot have children. The world has made a name for itself and failed; in the next chapter God will promise to make a name for Abram.
historical:
Shinar is the biblical name for Babylonia, the flat alluvial plain of southern Mesopotamia. The city is Babel, the Hebrew name for Babylon. Mesopotamian cities were dominated by ziggurats, massive stepped towers of mud brick with a shrine at the top, where heaven and earth were thought to meet. Babylon's own ziggurat was named Etemenanki, the temple of the foundation of heaven and earth. The Babylonian creation epic Enuma Elish ends with the gods themselves making bricks and building Babylon and its temple for their king Marduk, and the Babylonians understood the city's name to mean gate of the god. Genesis tells a different story about the same city: it was built by proud humans, and God had to come down to see it.

The second half of the chapter introduces Abram's family. Ur was an ancient and wealthy city in southern Mesopotamia, famous for its temple of the moon god and excavated by Leonard Woolley in the 1920s and 1930s. It is called Ur of the Chaldeans, using the name of a people who dominated southern Babylonia in the first millennium BC, which suggests the phrase was written or updated for later readers; some scholars have proposed a northern Ur nearer Haran. Haran, in what is now southeastern Turkey, was a trading city and another center of moon worship. Joshua 24:2 says plainly that Terah's family worshiped other gods beyond the Euphrates.
cultural:
Verse 3 notices something that would strike a reader in Canaan, where buildings were made of stone. In Mesopotamia, which had little stone, builders used mud brick, and for major buildings they fired the bricks in kilns and set them with bitumen, a natural tar that seeps from the ground in the region. The detail is accurate, and it also carries a hint of irony: these builders are using humble, man-made materials to reach the heavens.

In the ancient world, to make a name was to win lasting fame through great building projects and conquests; kings recorded their building works in inscriptions for exactly that reason. The builders want fame and security: a name, and protection from being scattered. Both desires run against God's command to fill the earth and against trust in God to give a name. In the genealogy that follows, the long lifespans continue to fall, from Shem's six hundred years to Nahor's one hundred forty-eight, and the chapter ends with Sarai's barrenness. In that world a childless marriage was a deep grief and seemed to close off the future of a family, which makes it the setting for God's promise.
literary: The Babel story is short and tightly built, and many scholars have observed that it forms a mirror pattern. The people speak (Come, let us make bricks), they build, and they state their goal; at the center, the LORD comes down to see; then God speaks (Come, let Us go down), confuses their language, and the building stops. The human let us in verses 3 and 4 is answered by the divine let Us in verse 7. Irony runs through it: the tower meant to reach heaven is so small that God must come down to look at it, and the people who built to avoid scattering are scattered. The chapter ends with a wordplay. The builders called the city Babel, gate of the god, but the Hebrew word sounds like balal, to confuse, and Genesis says that is where the LORD confused the language. The genealogy that follows begins with Shem, whose name means name, and runs ten generations to Abram, matching the ten from Adam to Noah in chapter 5. Like that list, it closes with a father of three sons (Terah, as Noah was), after which the story turns. Luke's genealogy of Jesus includes an extra name, Cainan, between Arphaxad and Shelah (Luke 3:36), following the ancient Greek translation of Genesis, a reminder that such lists were not always handed down identically.

outline.t: One language, and a city and tower to make a name
The LORD comes down, confuses language, and scatters them
The line of Shem from the flood to Terah
Terah's family: Abram, Sarai's barrenness, and the move to Haran

doctrines.note: The sin at Babel is pride organized on a grand scale: human beings uniting to secure their own name and future without God. It is the same impulse as the first sin, the desire to be like God, now built into a city. The chapter shows that sin is not only individual but can be expressed in cultures, projects, and institutions.

God's judgment on Babel is measured. He does not destroy the builders but confuses their language and scatters them, which stops the project and restrains the evil a united humanity could do. Judgment here also serves God's original command to fill the earth.

Humanity's greatest achievement is so small that God has to come down to see it. Whatever people build, God remains above it, able to halt it with a word. The chapter reassures readers who lived under the shadow of Babylon's power that God is not impressed by empires.

The genealogy quietly carries the promise forward. Out of the scattered nations, God keeps track of one line from Shem to Abram. The chapter ends with a barren woman, setting up a story in which God's purpose will depend entirely on his power to give life.

words.note: Balal, to mix or confuse. It is used elsewhere of mixing flour with oil for offerings. Here it describes God mixing up human speech so people cannot understand one another. Genesis connects it by sound with Babel, turning Babylon's proud name into a byword for confusion.

Shem, name. The builders want to make a name for themselves (verse 4). The genealogy of Shem, whose name is this very word, follows immediately, and in 12:2 God promises Abram, I will make your name great. A lasting name is something God gives, not something humans can build.

Migdal, tower. The word can mean a watchtower or a fortified tower in a city wall. Here it is almost certainly the kind of temple tower known in Mesopotamia, whose top was thought to reach toward the heavens. The builders' tower represents human religion and power as a bid to reach God on human terms.

Aqar, barren. It is the key word of verse 30, repeated for emphasis in the next clause, she had no children. Sarai's barrenness is the first great obstacle to God's promise of offspring, and barren women who conceive by God's intervention become a pattern in Scripture: Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah, and, in the New Testament, Elizabeth.

christ: Christians have long read the day of Pentecost in Acts 2 as the reversal of Babel. When the Holy Spirit came on the disciples, Jews “from every nation under heaven” heard them, and “each one heard them speaking his own language” (Acts 2:5-6). At Babel one language was divided into many to scatter a proud humanity; at Pentecost the many languages are not erased but each becomes a vehicle for the same message about Christ. The New Testament does not say this in so many words, so it is a thematic reading, but the parallel is striking. The prophets had already looked for the day when God would “restore pure lips to the peoples, that all may call upon the name of the LORD” (Zephaniah 3:9). Babel's builders wanted a name; God gave Jesus “the name above all names” (Philippians 2:9), a name received through humility and the cross. Babylon remains in Scripture a picture of human pride set against God, and Revelation announces its end: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!” (Revelation 18:2). Meanwhile Abraham, whose family is introduced here, looked forward to a city whose architect and builder is God (Hebrews 11:10).

hard.q: Was God threatened by the tower, and why did he confuse human languages?
hard.a:
Verse 6 can sound as if God is worried that humans will become too powerful: nothing they devise will be beyond them. Some readers take this as God protecting his own position. But the story itself undercuts that reading, since the tower is so small that the LORD must come down to see it. Most interpreters understand God's concern as being for humanity rather than for himself. A united human race set on securing its own name apart from God would multiply evil, as the world before the flood had done, and God acts to limit what sin can accomplish when concentrated in one place and one power. On this reading, the scattering is both judgment and mercy.

There is also the question of history. Some take the story as a straightforward account of the origin of the world's languages. Others note that chapter 10 already describes peoples with their own languages and read chapter 11 as a story about Babylon in particular, a theological portrait of the city that would later destroy Jerusalem, told in terms of the whole world. Still others see a real event in early Mesopotamia behind the account. What the text insists on is that human pride cannot build its way to heaven, and that God rules over the nations it has scattered.

questions: The builders wanted to make a name for themselves and feel secure. In what ways do people today try to build their own significance and security apart from God?
The tower meant to reach heaven was so small God had to come down to see it. How does that picture change the way you view human achievements you find impressive or intimidating?
The chapter ends with Sarai, who had no children, on the eve of God's promise. What situations in your life look like dead ends, and what might it mean to wait for God there?
